questions.question: What is a Git branch and how is it implemented internally?
questions.title: What Is a Git Branch?
questions.direct_answer: A **Git branch** is a named, movable reference to a commit. Creating a branch adds a reference; it does not copy the working tree or commit history. With the traditional ref backend it may appear under `.git/refs/heads/`, or Git may store it in another ref format. `HEAD` normally names the branch currently checked out.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands a branch is a pointer to a commit, not a copy of files, and can connect that to HEAD and Git's shared object database
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing a branch duplicates the codebase, which makes freshers afraid to branch and unable to explain why branching is instant
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that a branch is a ref into a shared object graph, while the exact ref and object-ID storage is an implementation detail.

sections.title: A Branch Is a Pointer, Not a Copy
sections.content:
A **Git branch** is a name that points to one commit. It does not contain a separate copy of the project. The commits, trees, and file objects are shared by every branch.

Git stores branch names as **refs**. In the traditional files backend, an actively updated branch is commonly a loose ref such as `.git/refs/heads/feature-user-auth`; refs may also be packed, and newer repositories can use another ref backend. The object ID can use the repository's configured object format, so teaching a branch as a fixed 40-byte SHA-1 file is too narrow.

When you commit, Git creates a new commit and advances the current branch ref to it. `HEAD` normally remains a symbolic reference to that branch. This small-reference model is why creating and moving branches is fast and cheap compared with copying a project directory.

sections.title: How a Branch Works Internally
sections.content:
amber|Branch|~Named movable ref|points to one commit|does not copy project files|moves as new commits are made
blue|HEAD|~Current checkout|normally names the current branch|can directly name a commit|stored separately from branch refs
emerald|Object database|~Shared history|commits, trees and blobs|used by every branch|unchanged objects are reused
violet|Ref storage|~Managed by Git|loose refs or packed refs|object format may vary|inspect with Git commands

sections.title: Create a Branch and Inspect the Pointer
sections.content:
```bash
# Create and switch to a feature branch
git switch -c feature-user-auth

# Add a commit; the branch ref advances to it
git add src/main/java/com/example/UserService.java
git commit -m "feat: add user authentication service"

# Inspect through Git instead of assuming a ref-storage file
git show-ref --verify refs/heads/feature-user-auth
git symbolic-ref --short HEAD
# feature-user-auth
```

`git show-ref` works without relying on whether the ref is loose, packed, or stored by another supported backend.

sections.title: Misconception: branching is 'heavy' so work stays on main
sections.content:
```bash
# Fresher avoids branches, fearing they copy the repo
git switch main
# ...commits half-finished feature straight onto main...
git commit -m "WIP user auth, not done"
# main is now broken/unreleasable, and there's nothing to PR
```

sections.title: Reality: branches are cheap, so isolate every task
sections.content:
```bash
# A branch is cheap to create because it is a ref, not a copied tree
git switch -c feature-user-auth
git commit -m "feat: add user authentication service"
# The team's merge and review rules decide how this branch reaches main
```
*Use branches to isolate work when that matches the repository's workflow.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking branches copy files**: branches point into one shared object graph.
- **Assuming every ref is a 40-character file**: Git can pack refs and supports different object/ref formats. Use `git show-ref` or `git rev-parse` to inspect a ref.
- **Saying `HEAD` advances independently**: on a normal checkout, the branch ref advances and symbolic `HEAD` continues to name that branch.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **A branch is a movable ref** that points to a commit.
- **Creating a branch does not copy files or history**; branches share Git's object database.
- **`HEAD` normally names the current branch**; a detached `HEAD` directly identifies a commit.
- **Ref storage is an implementation detail**: a branch may be loose, packed, or stored by another supported backend.
- **A commit advances the current branch ref** while other branch refs stay where they are.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Git branch is a named, movable reference to a commit. It is not a second copy of the repository. All branches share the same commit graph and object database, so creating a branch is normally a small metadata operation.

For example, `git switch -c feature-user-auth` creates the branch at the current commit and checks it out. When I commit, Git creates a new commit whose parent is the previous tip, then updates `refs/heads/feature-user-auth` to the new object ID. The other branches do not move.

`HEAD` records the current checkout. In the usual case it is a symbolic ref to the current branch. In detached-HEAD mode it identifies a commit directly. With Git's traditional ref backend a branch may be visible as a file under `.git/refs/heads`, but refs can also be packed or stored differently, and object IDs are not universally fixed to SHA-1. The stable mental model is simply: a branch is a movable name for one commit.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git checkout -b' and 'git switch -c' for creating branches?
questions.title: git checkout -b vs git switch -c
questions.direct_answer: Both commands create a branch and switch to it. **`git checkout -b`** is the older multi-purpose form; **`git switch -c`**, introduced in Git 2.23, expresses a branch operation directly. `git checkout -b` remains valid, while `git switch -c` is often easier for a beginner to read.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows that both forms create and check out a branch, and understands why Git added the narrower switch and restore commands.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing git switch and git restore exist, so the candidate uses checkout for everything from older tutorials
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Git 2.23 and explain that checkout remains valid; the newer split mainly improves command clarity.

sections.title: Why Git Split checkout Into switch and restore
sections.content:
Both commands perform the same branch operation: create a new branch at a start point and check it out.

`git checkout` is an older multi-purpose command. Depending on its arguments, it can switch branches, detach `HEAD`, or restore paths. Git 2.23 introduced `git switch` for branch/check-out operations and `git restore` for restoring working-tree or index content. This gives each command a narrower name.

`git checkout -b feature-payment` is not wrong or obsolete; it remains useful in existing scripts and documentation. For new learners, `git switch -c feature-payment` often communicates intent more clearly. In either form, Git still protects changes according to the command's normal checkout safety checks.

sections.title: git checkout -b vs git switch -c
sections.content:
| Aspect | `git checkout -b` | `git switch -c` |
|---|---|---|
| Result | Create and check out a branch | Create and check out a branch |
| Command design | Multi-purpose checkout command | Focused on switching/checking out branches |
| Availability | Long-standing Git command | Added in Git 2.23 |
| Existing scripts | Common | May be unavailable on old Git installations |
| File restoration | Checkout also has path forms | Use `git restore` for paths |

sections.title: Old checkout vs Modern split
sections.content:
rose|git checkout|~Older multi-purpose command|switch branches|create with -b|detach HEAD|has path-restoration forms
emerald|git switch|~Branch-focused command|switch a branch|create with -c|detach with --detach|added in Git 2.23
blue|git restore|~Path-focused command|restore working tree|restore index with --staged|separate from switching branches
amber|Choice|~Same branch result|prefer clarity for learning|keep checkout for compatibility|check installed Git version

sections.title: Overloaded checkout: same verb, dangerously different jobs
sections.content:
```bash
# Create a branch...
git checkout -b feature-payment

# ...but the SAME command also discards file changes:
git checkout -- OrderService.java   # silently wipes your edits!

# One verb for branches AND files = easy to trigger by accident
```

sections.title: Modern split: one verb per job
sections.content:
```bash
# Branch work
git switch -c feature-payment
git switch main

# Path restoration is expressed separately
git restore OrderService.java
```
*The narrower command names make the intended operation easier to see; normal safety checks still matter.*

sections.title: When to Use Each
sections.content: Use `git switch -c` when the installed Git version supports it and you want the command to state that this is a branch operation. Use `git checkout -b` in older environments, existing scripts, or a team workflow that standardizes on it. Both are valid; the important distinction is that checkout has several modes while switch is branch-focused.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing `git switch` exists**: learning from pre-2019 tutorials leaves you fighting checkout's overloaded behavior.
- **Using checkout to discard files**: `git checkout -- file.java` works but `git restore file.java` says exactly what it does.
- **Mixing the two inconsistently**: switch for branches but checkout for files adds cognitive load — commit to switch + restore.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Both commands create and check out a new branch.**
- **`git checkout -b`** is the older, multi-purpose syntax.
- **`git switch -c`** is the branch-focused syntax added in Git 2.23.
- **`git restore`** is the newer path-restoration command.
- Choose based on clarity, team convention, and the Git versions you support.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`git checkout -b feature-payment` and `git switch -c feature-payment` both create the branch and check it out. The difference is command design, not the resulting branch.

`git checkout` is the older command and has several modes: it can switch branches, detach `HEAD`, and restore paths. Git 2.23 added `git switch` for branch operations and `git restore` for path restoration, so `switch -c` is often easier to read in new code or teaching material.

I would normally use `git switch -c` when the environment supports it, but `git checkout -b` remains valid and is common in older scripts. I would not claim that one creates a safer branch; both both use Git's checkout safety rules. The practical choice is clear intent versus compatibility.

questions.question: What is a feature branch workflow and why is it used?
questions.title: Feature Branch Workflow
questions.direct_answer: A **feature branch workflow** develops one change on a separate branch and later integrates it into a target branch, often through a pull request. It isolates incomplete work and creates a place for review and automated checks. Whether direct commits are allowed, reviews are required, or `main` is always deployable depends on the team's policy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the day-to-day team workflow: branch off main, PR, review, merge — and why each step exists
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing directly to main in a team setting, or branching from a stale main and hitting avoidable conflicts later
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that short-lived feature branches plus pull requests give you parallel work AND a review checkpoint, and that you should pull main before branching

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A feature or fix is developed on its own branch.
- The branch is pushed and commonly proposed through a pull request.
- Isolation lets several changes progress without placing every unfinished edit on the target branch.
- Review and CI can run before merge when the repository requires them.
- Branch lifetime, merge method, and protection rules are team choices—not Git guarantees.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A feature branch workflow puts one change—such as a feature, bug fix, or refactor—on a branch separate from the target branch. The developer commits there, pushes the branch, and commonly opens a pull request. Reviewers and CI can check that proposal before the team merges it.

For example, I might create `feature/customer-search` from the agreed base, make focused commits, push it, and open a PR into `main`. The separate branch keeps the unfinished change out of the target branch and gives the team a clear unit to discuss or test.

The workflow does not itself guarantee a deployable `main`, conflict-free parallel work, or mandatory review. Those outcomes depend on small branches, branch protection, CI, release practices, and team discipline. Some teams use trunk-based development instead. The useful idea is isolation plus an explicit integration point, not a universal ban on direct commits.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A feature branch is a temporary line of development for one coherent change. It starts from a chosen base commit, receives its own commits, and is later integrated into the target branch. Because the branch is just a ref into the shared commit graph, the workflow adds little Git storage overhead.

The pull request is a hosting-platform collaboration step, not a Git requirement. It shows the proposed diff, discussion, reviews, and checks. Repository rules may require approvals or passing CI, or the team may use a lighter process.

Short, focused branches usually reduce review size and divergence. Updating from the target branch can reveal conflicts earlier, but blindly running `git pull` before every branch is not a universal rule—teams may fetch and rebase, merge, or branch from a known remote ref. The workflow succeeds when its integration policy is explicit and the branch stays focused.

sections.title: The Feature Branch Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[git switch main
git pull] --> B[git switch -c
feature-x] B --> C[code + commit] C --> D[git push
feature-x] D --> E[open PR
review + CI] E --> F[merge to main] F --> G[delete branch] ```

sections.title: The Workflow Step by Step
sections.content:
```bash
# 1. Start from an up-to-date main
git switch main
git pull origin main

# 2. Create a feature branch
git switch -c feature-add-customer-search

# 3. Develop + commit (e.g. a new CustomerSearchService)
git add src/main/java/com/example/service/CustomerSearchService.java
git commit -m "feat: add case-insensitive customer search"

# 4. Push the branch to the remote
git push origin feature-add-customer-search

# 5. Open a pull request -> review + CI run
# 6. After approval, merge to main, then clean up
git switch main && git pull origin main
git branch -d feature-add-customer-search
```

sections.title: Anti-pattern: committing straight to main
sections.content:
```bash
# Fresher treats main as a personal scratch pad
git switch main
git add .
git commit -m "add search + random unrelated tweak"
git push origin main
# No review, breaks CI expecting PRs, conflicts with teammates pushing to main
```

sections.title: Correct: one task, one short-lived branch, one PR
sections.content:
```bash
git switch main && git pull origin main   # always start fresh
git switch -c feature-add-customer-search
git commit -am "feat: add case-insensitive customer search"
git push origin feature-add-customer-search
# Open a PR -> teammates review, CI runs, then merge
```
*One focused branch per task, pulled from a fresh main, keeps conflicts small and reviews meaningful.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Ignoring repository policy**: use the branch, review, and protection rules agreed by the team.
- **One giant long-lived branch**: a single `my-work` branch with unrelated changes defeats isolation; one task per branch.
- **Starting from an outdated base**: fetch first and use the team's rebase or merge policy to limit unnecessary divergence.
- **Self-merging without review**: approving your own PR throws away the safety net the workflow exists for.

questions.question: How do you list, create, and delete branches in Git?
questions.title: Managing Git Branches: List, Create, Delete
questions.direct_answer: Use **`git branch`** to list local branches, **`git branch -a`** to include remote-tracking branches, **`git switch -c <name>`** (or `git branch <name>`) to create, and **`git branch -d <name>`** to delete a merged branch. The lowercase **`-d`** is safe — it refuses to drop unmerged work — while **`-D`** force-deletes regardless.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the everyday branch commands and the safety difference between -d and -D
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for -D as a 'stronger delete' and discarding unmerged commits, or forgetting -a when hunting for a teammate's remote branch
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that -d protects you by refusing to delete unmerged branches, that force-deleted commits are often recoverable via reflog, and that -r lists remote-tracking branches only

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`git branch`** lists local; **`-a`** adds remote-tracking; **`-r`** is remote-only.
- **`git switch -c <name>`** creates and switches in one step.
- **`git branch -d`** is safe — refuses unmerged branches.
- **`git branch -D`** force-deletes regardless — use cautiously.
- **`git reflog`** can often recover commits after an accidental force-delete.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: There are three everyday operations: listing, creating, and deleting branches. To list them, you run git branch, which shows your local branches with an asterisk next to the one you're on. If you also want to see remote branches — say, something a teammate pushed — you add dash a, so git branch dash a, and that shows local plus remote-tracking branches. To create a branch, you can use git branch with a name to just create it, but more commonly you'd use git switch dash c with a name, which creates the branch and switches to it in one step. For deleting, there's an important safety distinction. Lowercase git branch dash d deletes a branch, but it's safe — it refuses if the branch has commits that haven't been merged yet, which protects you from losing work. Uppercase dash D force-deletes regardless, so you should only use it when you're certain you don't need that work. Always try the lowercase version first. In practice you'd delete feature branches after they're merged to keep your branch list tidy. The mistakes freshers make are reaching for dash D as if it's just a stronger delete and losing commits, and forgetting dash a when looking for a remote branch, so they think it doesn't exist when it's actually on origin. And if you ever do force-delete something by accident, git reflog can usually help you recover the commit.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Use `git branch` to inspect and manage branch refs, and `git switch` to change the checked-out branch. Plain `git branch` lists local branches; `git branch -r` lists remote-tracking refs; `git branch -a` shows both groups.

`git branch topic` creates a branch without switching, while `git switch -c topic` creates and checks it out. `git branch -d topic` checks that the branch is fully merged into its configured upstream, or into `HEAD` when no suitable upstream is configured. `git branch -D topic` bypasses that merged check.

Deleting a branch deletes its ref, not all objects immediately. Unreferenced commits may still be recoverable through the reflog for a time, but recovery should not replace checking the branch before deletion.

sections.title: Branch Commands at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|List|~See what exists|git branch (local)|git branch -a (all)|git branch -r (remote)
emerald|Create|~Start new work|git branch name|git switch -c name|switch -c also moves you
rose|Delete|~Clean up|git branch -d (safe)|git branch -D (force)|-d refuses unmerged work
amber|Inspect|~Know your context|* marks current branch|run before committing|avoids wrong-branch commits

sections.title: List, Create, and Delete in One Session
sections.content:
```bash
# List local branches (current marked with *)
git branch
#   feature-payment
# * main

# Include remote-tracking branches
git branch -a
# * main
#   remotes/origin/main
#   remotes/origin/feature-payment

# Create + switch in one command
git switch -c feature-add-notifications

# After the PR merges, delete safely from main
git switch main
git branch -d feature-payment        # works only if merged

# Safe delete refuses unmerged work:
git branch -d bugfix-wip
# error: branch 'bugfix-wip' is not fully merged

# Force delete only if you're sure
git branch -D bugfix-wip             # use with caution
```

sections.title: Mistake: force-deleting and losing unmerged commits
sections.content:
```bash
# Fresher treats -D as 'delete harder' and skips the safety check
git branch -D feature-half-done
# Unmerged commits are gone from branch refs
# (recoverable via reflog only if you act fast)
```

sections.title: Safe: let -d guard your work
sections.content:
```bash
# Try the safe delete first
git branch -d feature-half-done
# error: not fully merged  <- Git just saved you

# Merge or back it up first, THEN delete
git switch main && git merge feature-half-done
git branch -d feature-half-done      # now safe
```
*If you ever do force-delete by accident, `git reflog` can usually recover the lost commit hash.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `-D` blindly**: it skips the unmerged-work safety check and can lose commits — try `-d` first.
- **Not cleaning up merged branches**: stale branches pile up and clutter `git branch` — delete after merge.
- **Forgetting `-a`**: plain `git branch` hides remote branches, so a teammate's pushed branch looks 'missing'.

questions.question: What is the HEAD pointer in Git?
questions.title: The HEAD Pointer in Git
questions.direct_answer: **`HEAD`** identifies the current checkout. It is usually a symbolic reference to the current branch, such as `refs/heads/main`; in detached-HEAD mode it directly identifies a commit. A normal commit advances the branch ref that `HEAD` names, while `HEAD` continues to name that branch.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands HEAD as a local 'current position' pointer and can explain detached HEAD state
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing HEAD with the remote or with main specifically, or panicking in detached HEAD without knowing commits there can be lost
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that HEAD is stored in .git/HEAD as a ref, that HEAD~1 references prior commits, and that you save detached-HEAD work by branching from it

sections.title: HEAD Is Your 'You Are Here' Marker
sections.content:
**`HEAD`** is the pointer Git uses to track your current position — which branch or commit you currently have checked out. Most of the time it points to a **branch name**, and that branch points to a commit.

It's stored as a file at `.git/HEAD`, usually containing something like `ref: refs/heads/main`. When you commit, Git advances the current branch ref; `HEAD` continues to resolve through that branch. When you `git switch` to another branch, `HEAD` updates to point at it. Commands like `git log` start from `HEAD`. Understanding it matters because Git error messages constantly mention `HEAD`, and concepts like **detached HEAD** only make sense once you see that `HEAD` is just a pointer that can aim at different things.

sections.title: HEAD States at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Normal HEAD|~Points to a branch|.git/HEAD = ref: refs/heads/main|moves with commits|the everyday case
amber|Detached HEAD|~Points to a commit|happens on checkout <hash>|new commits initially unnamed|fine for read-only
emerald|Relative refs|~Walk backwards|HEAD~1 = one commit back|HEAD~3 = three back|used in reset/diff
rose|Local only|~Per-developer|not synced to origin|each repo has its own|nothing remote about it

sections.title: Normal vs Detached HEAD
sections.content:
```bash
# Normal: HEAD points to a branch
git switch main
cat .git/HEAD            # ref: refs/heads/main

git commit -am "feat: add order persistence"
git log --oneline -1
# a3f2b9c (HEAD -> main) feat: add order persistence

# Detached HEAD: check out a raw commit hash
git checkout a3f2b9c
# Note: switching to 'a3f2b9c'. You are in 'detached HEAD' state.
git log --oneline -1
# a3f2b9c (HEAD) feat: add order persistence   <- no branch name!

# Save detached work by branching, or just go back
git switch -c experiment   # keep any commits made here
git switch main            # back to normal
```

sections.title: Trap: committing in detached HEAD and losing it
sections.content:
```bash
git checkout a3f2b9c          # detached HEAD
git commit -am "fix: quick experiment"
git switch main              # walked away...
# The experiment commit has no branch name -> easy to stop seeing
```

sections.title: Fix: branch first, then commit
sections.content:
```bash
git checkout a3f2b9c          # detached HEAD
git switch -c experiment      # attach a branch BEFORE committing
git commit -am "fix: quick experiment"
# Now the commit lives on 'experiment' and is safe
```
*Detached HEAD is safe for read-only investigation — just create a branch before making commits you care about.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing `HEAD` with `main`**: `HEAD` is wherever you currently are; on `feature-auth` it points there, not to `main`.
- **Thinking `HEAD` is remote**: it's purely local — each clone has its own `HEAD`.
- **Panicking in detached HEAD**: it's safe to look around; just branch before committing anything you want to keep.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`HEAD` identifies the current checkout.**
- Normally it is a symbolic ref to the current branch.
- In detached-HEAD mode it directly identifies a commit.
- A normal commit advances the current branch ref; symbolic `HEAD` continues to name it.
- Create a branch before leaving detached HEAD if you want a durable name for new commits.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: HEAD is a special pointer in Git that tracks your current position in the repository — it's basically your 'you are here' marker. At any moment, HEAD points to whatever branch you currently have checked out, and that branch points to a commit. Git stores HEAD as a file in the dot-git folder, and inside it you'll usually see something like 'ref colon refs slash heads slash main', meaning HEAD is pointing to the main branch. When you make a commit, Git automatically moves both HEAD and your current branch forward to the new commit. When you switch branches, HEAD moves to point at the new branch. This is how Git always knows where you are and where new commits should go. HEAD shows up constantly in Git messages, like 'HEAD is now at' some commit, and once you know it's just your position marker, those messages make sense. One special case is detached HEAD state. That happens when you check out a specific commit hash instead of a branch name, so HEAD points directly at that commit rather than a branch. It's called detached because you're not on any branch. That's totally fine for looking at old code, but if you make commits there, they don't belong to any branch and can be lost. So if you want to keep work done in detached HEAD, you create a branch from that point first. A common mistake freshers make is thinking HEAD is the same as main or that it has something to do with the remote — it doesn't. HEAD is purely local and just tracks wherever you currently are.

items: Normally HEAD points to a branch and moves forward when you commit.
If you check out a raw commit hash, you're in detached HEAD state.
HEAD is local only — it has nothing to do with the remote.

beats.text: If I check out an old commit to investigate a bug, HEAD detaches and points straight at that commit. If I want to keep any changes I make there, I create a branch first, otherwise those commits can get lost.

items: Don't confuse HEAD with main or with the remote.
Don't commit in detached HEAD without branching first.
